documents.body:
20 y/o M, college student, heading into his junior year, runs distance and middle distance on the track team. Wanted one doctor he could text while at school. Last primary care was his pediatrician in Connecticut, records release signed today.

No complaints. No chronic problems, never hospitalized, no surgeries. No meds, no supplements. NKDA.

FH: father died suddenly at 41. Pt doesn't know the cause, was never told details. No other family history he can name today.
SH: lives in campus housing during the year, home in Deerfield in the summers. Never smoked, no vaping. Drinks occasionally at social events, a few drinks a month. No drugs.

ROS negative, specifically no chest pain, palpitations, fainting or trouble keeping up at practice.

Exam: vitals as charted. Lean, well appearing. HEENT clear. Neck supple, no adenopathy. Heart regular rate and rhythm, S1 S2 normal, no murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. Extremities without edema, pulses 2+ and symmetric. Skin clear. Neuro grossly normal.

PHQ-2 0. AUDIT-C 2.

A/P
1. Health maintenance, healthy 20 y/o. One-time HIV and hep C screening today, plus CBC, CMP and lipids as a baseline. Vaccine history pending pediatric records; will catch up flu and COVID in the fall.
2. Family history of sudden death in father, cause unknown. Asked him to find out what he can from family.

RTC one year, or sooner as needed. Gave him the practice cell number.

documents.title: Office Visit - Collapse
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Texted me last night, I asked him to come in first thing.

S: Yesterday afternoon during interval repeats at indoor practice he felt a brief tight feeling in his chest, then the next thing he knew he was on the track with teammates and the coach over him. Teammates say he was out only briefly, no shaking reported, didn't bite his tongue, no incontinence. Came around quickly and was clear. Coach wanted him to go to the ED; he declined and walked back to the dorm. Fine since. No chest pain now, no palpitations he noticed. Never happened before. Ate and drank normally that day.

No meds. NKDA.
FH: father died suddenly at 41, still doesn't know more.

O: Vitals as charted. Well, comfortable. Heart regular, there is a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that I did not hear in August. No gallop. Lungs clear. No edema. Neuro nonfocal.
ECG in office: NSR, normal intervals, no LVH, no Q waves, no ST-T changes. Normal.

A/P: Syncope with exertion, preceded by chest tightness, new murmur, and a father who died suddenly young. Normal ECG doesn't reassure me enough. Urgent cardiology referral today for consult and echo. No running, lifting or hard exertion until cardiology sees him; he'll tell his coach and I'll write a note. If anything recurs, chest pain, palpitations or near-fainting, he goes straight to the ED, not to me.
Discussed with him for a while, he understands why.

medications.drug: 24 HR metoprolol succinate 50 MG Extended Release Oral Tablet

reports.text: Complete 2D, M-mode, color and spectral Doppler study. Left ventricle normal in cavity size. Asymmetric hypertrophy of the interventricular septum, maximal septal wall thickness 21 mm; posterior wall 10 mm. Left ventricular systolic function hyperdynamic, LVEF 70% by visual estimate. Systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral leaflet. Resting LVOT peak gradient 38 mmHg, increasing to 64 mmHg with Valsalva. Mitral and aortic valves structurally normal. Tricuspid and pulmonic valves normal. Right ventricle normal in size and function. Atria normal in size. No pericardial effusion. IVC normal with normal respiratory variation.
reports.conclusion: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (resting 38 mmHg, 64 mmHg with Valsalva), consistent with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. LVEF 70%. No structural valvular abnormality.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outpatient cardiology consultation
Date of visit: 03/13/2023
Referring: primary care physician
Reason: syncope during exercise

Dear colleague,

Thank you for asking me to see Rowan, a 20-year-old university student and track athlete. On 3/2 during an interval workout he had a short-lived sensation of chest tightness and then lost consciousness, coming around quickly on the track. He had no prior episodes. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. No known drug allergies.

Family history: he spoke with his family this past week. His father died suddenly at 41; the family has understood it as a cardiac death. A paternal uncle carries a diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Social: never smoker, occasional alcohol on weekends, no drug use. Full-time student.

Vital signs were stable today. On exam he is a fit young man in no distress. JVP not elevated. There is a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Lungs clear. No peripheral edema.

Echocardiogram today shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy (21 mm septum, 10 mm posterior wall) with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a resting outflow gradient of 38 mmHg that rises to 64 mmHg with Valsalva. Ejection fraction 70%. The valves themselves are structurally normal.

Impression: Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, presenting with exertional syncope.

Plan:
1. Start metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Prescription sent.
2. He should stay out of competitive running and strenuous exertion. We talked at length about what that means for his season; light recreational activity is fine.
3. Stay well hydrated and avoid dehydration and heavy alcohol use, both of which worsen obstruction.
4. Return to clinic in one year, sooner for any recurrent symptoms.

Allergies: NKDA
Medications at end of visit: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily

Sincerely,
Outpatient cardiology

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Date of service: 03/06/2024, arrived 16:35 by private vehicle with friends
PCP: primary care physician, copy sent

CHIEF COMPLAINT: passing out, more than once

HPI: 21 y/o M with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosed last year after he collapsed at track practice, on metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Presents after another fainting spell this afternoon. Describes several similar spells: he gets queasy, hot and lightheaded, and then goes down. This afternoon he was with friends, who say he went pale and sweaty and then slumped to the floor; he came around within moments. No injury, no tongue biting, no incontinence, no post-event confusion. No chest pain, no palpitations, no exertion at the time of any of the spells. Denies drug use.

PMH: obstructive HCM. PSH: none. Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father with sudden cardiac death at 41; paternal uncle with HCM.
SH: university student, never smoker, occasional alcohol, none today.

EXAM: BP 120/75, HR 70 at triage. Alert, oriented x3, no distress. No head or facial trauma. Heart regular, systolic murmur at the LLSB. Lungs clear. Abdomen benign. Neuro: nonfocal, gait normal.

ECG (asymptomatic): normal sinus rhythm, no abnormalities.
Labs: CBC, BMP and high-sensitivity troponin within normal limits.

ED COURSE: Placed on continuous cardiac monitoring. At about 18:10, while seated on the stretcher, he said he felt the same nausea and warmth coming on and became pale. The monitor showed sinus bradycardia followed by a brief period of asystole, then return to normal sinus rhythm as he came around. He was laid flat and recovered within a minute, no intervention needed. Cardiology was consulted by phone and reviewed the strip. He remained on telemetry for the rest of his stay without another event.

MDM: Recurrent syncope with a prodrome of nausea, warmth and lightheadedness, and a captured episode showing sinus bradycardia and a brief pause. Background obstructive HCM. Normal resting ECG and labs. Cardiology agrees with discharge with early outpatient follow-up and no medication change tonight.

DIAGNOSIS: Syncope.

DISPOSITION: Discharged home at 23:50 in the care of friends. Continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Cardiology clinic will call him for a visit within two weeks. Return precautions given: chest pain, palpitations, fainting with exertion, or any injury from a fall.

Emergency medicine attending

documents.title: Cardiology Follow-up
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Cardiology clinic follow-up
Date of visit: 03/18/2024

Dear colleague,

I saw Rowan again after his ED visit on 3/6 for recurrent fainting. He describes several episodes, all while standing or sitting still, each heralded by nausea, warmth and lightheadedness and followed by a brief loss of consciousness. None have been exertional and none came with chest pain or palpitations. The episode captured on ED telemetry showed sinus bradycardia and a brief asystolic pause with spontaneous recovery, coinciding with his usual prodrome. No episodes since the ED.

Medications: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.

Today he looks well. Vital signs as recorded. The systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border is unchanged. Lungs clear, no edema.

Echo today is unchanged from last year: septum 21 mm, EF 70%, outflow gradient 36 mmHg at rest and 60 mmHg with Valsalva.

Impression:
1. Recurrent syncope. The prodrome and the setting, together with the bradycardia and pause during a typical spell, favor a reflex mechanism rather than an outflow or arrhythmic event.
2. Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, stable by echo.

Plan:
1. Continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, no change.
2. Generous fluid intake. At the first sign of the warning feeling, sit or lie down; leg-crossing and hand-grip counter-pressure maneuvers reviewed and practiced in clinic.
3. Continue to avoid competitive and strenuous exertion.
4. Return in one year, sooner for any exertional symptoms or recurrent syncope.

Sincerely,
Outpatient cardiology

conditions.label: Traumatic epidural hemorrhage with loss of consciousness of unspecified duration, initial encounter

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily for 7 days total (last dose 3/12)
Take 2 tablets by mouth every 8 hours as needed for pain

reports.text:
Indication: motorcycle crash, unhelmeted, loss of consciousness at scene, severe headache.
Technique: axial noncontrast CT of the head with coronal and sagittal reformats.
Findings: Hyperdense biconvex extra-axial collection over the right temporal convexity that does not cross suture lines, maximal thickness 16 mm, estimated volume 34 mL. Local mass effect with 3 mm leftward midline shift. Basal cisterns patent. No subdural, subarachnoid or intraparenchymal hemorrhage. No fracture identified. Ventricles normal in size. Gray-white differentiation preserved. Paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells clear.
reports.conclusion: Acute right temporal epidural hematoma, 16 mm maximal thickness, approximately 34 mL, with 3 mm midline shift. No other intracranial hemorrhage. No fracture identified. Neurosurgery notified at 15:31.

reports.text:
Comparison: 03/06/2026.
Findings: Interval right temporal craniotomy with evacuation of the epidural hematoma. Expected postoperative pneumocephalus and soft tissue swelling at the operative site. No residual or recurrent epidural collection. No new intracranial hemorrhage. Midline shift resolved. Basal cisterns patent.
reports.conclusion: Satisfactory evacuation of right temporal epidural hematoma. No residual or new hemorrhage.

documents.title: Neurosurgery Admission History and Physical
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
NEUROSURGERY ADMISSION H&P
Date of service: 03/06/2026, 15:40

CC: severe headache after motorcycle crash

HPI: 23 y/o man with obstructive HCM and a history of syncope, brought in by EMS after a motorcycle crash. He was not wearing a helmet. Found unresponsive at the scene by bystanders and EMS; he woke up shortly after arrival in our ED and now complains of a severe headache. No other complaints.

PMH: obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; syncope (2024).
PSH: none.
Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, last dose this morning.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father sudden cardiac death at 41; paternal uncle with HCM.
SH: university student. Never smoker. Occasional alcohol.

Exam: BP 140/90, HR 100, RR 18, T 37.0 C (98.6 F), SpO2 98% RA.
Alert and oriented to person, place and time but restless on the stretcher. Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Face symmetric. Full strength throughout, sensation intact, no drift. No focal neurologic deficit. Cervical collar in place, cleared after CT. Primary and secondary trauma survey otherwise negative per ED.

Imaging: CT head, acute right temporal epidural hematoma, biconvex, not crossing sutures, 16 mm thick, about 34 mL, 3 mm midline shift. CT C-spine negative.
Labs: CBC, BMP, PT/INR normal.

Assessment: Traumatic epidural hematoma, right temporal, volume over 30 mL with mass effect, after loss of consciousness at the scene.

Plan: Emergent right temporal craniotomy for evacuation. Consent obtained from the patient, mother present and informed. Anesthesia aware of obstructive HCM: maintain preload, avoid tachycardia and vasodilation. Continue metoprolol. Levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis. Neuro ICU postoperatively.

Neurosurgery attending

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT
Date of surgery: 03/06/2026
Preoperative diagnosis: right temporal epidural hematoma
Postoperative diagnosis: same
Procedure: right temporal craniotomy for evacuation of epidural hematoma
Anesthesia: general endotracheal
EBL: minimal
Specimens: none
Complications: none

Indications: 23 y/o man after an unhelmeted motorcycle crash with an acute right temporal epidural hematoma of about 34 mL with midline shift.

Description: Supine, head turned left on a horseshoe rest. Right temporal question-mark incision after prep and drape. Scalp flap reflected, bone flap turned with the craniotome. Acute epidural clot encountered and evacuated with suction and irrigation. Bleeding points coagulated. Dura intact, tacked up circumferentially. Hemostasis confirmed. Bone flap replaced with plates. Subgaleal drain placed. Galea closed with interrupted sutures, skin with staples. Sterile dressing.

The patient tolerated the procedure well, extubated in the OR, moving all extremities, to the neuro ICU in stable condition. Anesthesia reported stable hemodynamics on preload support; metoprolol continued.

Neurosurgery attending

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 03/06/2026  Discharged: 03/10/2026
Service: Neurosurgery

Principal diagnosis: traumatic right temporal epidural hematoma
Other: obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; history of syncope
Procedure: right temporal craniotomy with evacuation of epidural hematoma, 03/06/2026

Course: Arrived after an unhelmeted motorcycle crash with loss of consciousness at the scene, regaining consciousness in the ED, with severe headache and a 34 mL right temporal epidural hematoma on CT. Taken emergently to the OR the same afternoon for craniotomy and evacuation, uncomplicated. Postoperative day 1 CT showed satisfactory evacuation without residual or new hemorrhage. Two nights in the neuro ICU, then the neurosurgery floor. Drain removed POD 1. Neurologically intact throughout. Headache settled to mild by POD 2 on acetaminophen alone. Levetiracetam for 7 days of seizure prophylaxis. Metoprolol continued at home dose with stable heart rate and blood pressure. Ambulating independently, tolerating diet. CT cervical spine negative; no other injuries identified.

Condition at discharge: good. Alert, oriented, no focal deficit. Incision clean, staples in place.

Allergies: NKDA

Discharge medications:
- Metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily (unchanged)
- Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, last dose 03/12/2026
- Acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed for pain

Instructions: no heavy lifting or contact activity until neurosurgery follow-up. Keep the incision dry for 48 hours, then gentle washing. Staple removal in 7 to 10 days, at the PCP office is fine. Wear a helmet when riding. Return for worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, weakness or seizure.

Follow-up: neurosurgery clinic in about 4 weeks with CT head. PCP within one week.

Neurosurgery

documents.title: Post-hospital visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-discharge. Admitted 3/6 to 3/10 at an outside hospital, neurosurgery service: unhelmeted motorcycle crash, LOC at the scene, right temporal epidural hematoma about 34 mL with 3 mm shift, emergent right temporal craniotomy and evacuation same day. POD1 CT clean. Discharge summary, op note and H&P reviewed.

Today: here with his mother. Headache gone the last day or so, took acetaminophen once yesterday. No nausea, vomiting, confusion, weakness, numbness or vision change. Sleeping fine. Finished levetiracetam last night. Still on metoprolol succinate 50 daily. No syncope.

Meds: metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily; acetaminophen 1000 mg q8h prn. NKDA.

Exam: vitals as charted. Alert, oriented, conversational, appropriate. Right temporal curvilinear incision with staples, clean, dry, no erythema or drainage, no fluid collection. Pupils equal and reactive, EOM full, face symmetric, strength and sensation normal, gait steady. Heart regular, systolic murmur LLSB as before. Lungs clear.

A/P
1. Traumatic epidural hematoma s/p craniotomy 3/6, recovering well, intact. Staples out Tuesday 3/17 with nursing. Neurosurgery f/u with CT in April, scheduled. Activity per neurosurgery: no lifting or contact. Helmet, every time, if he rides again; we talked about it plainly.
2. Obstructive HCM: stable through the admission. Cardiology annual had been booked for March; he'll reschedule after neurosurgery clears him.
3. Med rec done.

documents.title: Staple removal
documents.author: RN
documents.body: 11 days post right temporal craniotomy. Staples removed without difficulty. Incision well approximated and healed along its length, no erythema, drainage or gaps. Steri-strips not needed. Pt feels well, no headache. Told him he can wash his hair normally now. Reminded about neurosurgery visit in April.

documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Neurosurgery clinic
Date of visit: 04/13/2026

Dear colleague,

Rowan is five weeks out from right temporal craniotomy for evacuation of a traumatic epidural hematoma. He feels back to normal. No headaches, no seizures, no new neurological symptoms. He is attending classes. Medications: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: incision fully healed, flap contour good. Alert and oriented, speech fluent, cranial nerves intact, strength and sensation normal, gait normal.

CT head today: resolution of the epidural hematoma; postoperative changes only.

Impression: traumatic epidural hematoma, resolved after evacuation. Excellent recovery.

Plan: cleared for normal activity, including classes and exercise within his cardiology limits. We discussed helmet use at length. No routine neurosurgical follow-up needed; we are happy to see him again for any concerns.

Sincerely,
Neurosurgery

From a cardiac standpoint he has had no syncope since March 2024 and no exertional chest pain, dyspnea or palpitations. Medications: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vital signs as recorded. Healed right temporal scar. Systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, unchanged. Lungs clear. No edema.

Echo today: septum 21 mm, EF 70%, outflow gradient 35 mmHg at rest and 62 mmHg with Valsalva, unchanged.

Impression: obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, stable. Syncope, no recurrence.

Plan: continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Activity guidance unchanged. Return in one year.

Sincerely,
Outpatient cardiology
